paper_title: TCP4D: A Unified Tool-Center-Point Tracking and Generation Model for Robot Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large-scale video data of robot manipulation (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2023; Contributors et al., 2026) offer rich source of experience for learning diverse skills. These data provide an important foundation for modern vision-language-action (VLA) models (Pan et al., 2026; Intelligence et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026c) and world action models (WAMs) (Ye et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026b; Su et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026), whose training relies on action supervision. However, not all videos include synchronized action annotations, and recovering these labels from RGB video alone remains nontrivial challenge. Recovering the end effectors motion offers practical route to obtaining such supervision from videos. This motion can be represented by the tool-center-point (TCP) pose (i.e., SE(3)), which specifies the position and orientation of the end effectors tool frame. With common reference frame, TCP provides unified action representation: the same pose encodes the same task-space goal across robot platforms, even when their joint configurations differ, since each robot can reach the pose through its own inverse kinematics (IK) (Xiaomi Embodied Intelligence Team et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026) if within its work range. Recent 4D point tracking methods (Luo et al., 2026; Karhade et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Sucar et al., 2026) recover scene geometry and track 3D surface points from RGB video. The TCP, however, is the origin of virtual tool frame and can lie in free space between the gripper fingers. Its image projection can therefore fall on background pixel. Moreover, point trackers predict only 3D positions not tool orientation, so even an accurate trajectory of the TCP origin does not determine the full TCP pose. Recovering full TCP poses from these trackers therefore relies on additional robot-specific priors and multi-stage post-processing, along which errors accumulate and may lead to inaccurate poses or tracking failures. To address this challenge, we propose TCP4D, unified model that tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories from shared 4D scene representation. Given monocular RGB video and an initial 2D TCP query for each arm, the Tracker directly estimates TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states throughout the observed sequence, together with metric scene geometry and camera parameters, without additional robot priors or post-processing. The Tracker further adapts to new embodiments in few-shot manner. TCP poses provide an action interface for robot control, allowing predicted future TCP trajectories to be executed as robot actions. The Generator extracts local visual features along the tracked motion. Diffusion Transformer (DiT) combines these features with the shared scene representation to generate task-conditioned future TCP and gripper states, serving as manipulation policy. Since the recovered TCP motion is embodiment-agnostic, TCP4D further enables novel crossembodiment data augmentation pipeline that converts existing RGB videos of source robot into demonstrations for target embodiments. Unlike existing methods that require recorded source-robot states (Chen et al., 2024b; Ji et al., 2025), our pipeline recovers TCP trajectories and gripper states directly from video, removes the source robot via segmentation and inpainting, and renders the target embodiment driven by the recovered trajectory through IK. single video thus yields demonstrations for any target embodiment that can reach the recovered motion, without additional data collection. Extensive experiments validate TCP4D on TCP tracking, manipulation, and cross-embodiment data augmentation. For tracking, TCP4D achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab, respectively, and 8.85 mm on the UR5 using just ten demonstrations. As manipulation policy, it achieves 69.19% average success on RoboTwin and 78.33% across two real-world tasks. Joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves success rates on both source and target robots. Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce TCP4D, unified model that directly recovers TCP poses and gripper states from RGB videos and generates future TCP trajectories conditioned on observations and instructions. TCP4D adapts effectively to new robot embodiment with only few demonstrations. We develop novel cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline that transforms RGB demonstrations into target-robot training data through recovered TCP motion, without requiring recorded sourcerobot state trajectories. 2 Extensive experiments across diverse tasks in simulation benchmarks and real-world settings demonstrate the strong performance of TCP4D in TCP tracking and manipulation, as well as the effectiveness of its cross-embodiment data augmentation.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 4D Reconstruction and Point Tracking. Recent feed-forward approaches to 4D reconstruction include dense geometric prediction (Wang et al., 2026b; Peng et al., 2026; Sucar et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026) and query-based frameworks (Zhang et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026) that provide flexible access to scene geometry and motion across space and time. Beyond tracking observed motion, recent methods (Zhang et al., 2026b; Duisterhof et al., 2026) predict future point-cloud dynamics through 3D trajectory forecasting and completion. These approaches primarily characterize scene geometry and point positions, leaving local orientation implicit. Concurrent work MoSE3 (Cheng et al., 2026) extends motion estimation to dense per-pixel SE(3) transforms by fitting rigid motions within soft clusters of tracked scene points. In contrast, TCP4D directly tracks the SE(3) pose of virtual TCP, without requiring corresponding physical surface point or rigid-body grouping. Point-based Manipulation Policy. Prior work uses predicted 2D point tracks to guide manipulation policies (Bharadhwaj et al., 2024a; Cao et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2024). In 3D, world models predict geometric motion to support planning and action learning (Zhi et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026d; Hu et al., 2026). Other approaches infer waypoints or poses from visual predictions (Huang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025), or incorporate motion cues into VLA policies (Wang et al., 2026a; Yuan et al., 2026a). Point-based policies also use depth-derived scene geometry to ground action prediction. DP3 (Ze et al., 2024) conditions action diffusion on compact features from sparse point clouds, while Act3D (Gervet et al., 2023) searches 3D feature field for the next end-effector position. 3D Diffuser Actor (Ke et al., 2024) denoises pose trajectories conditioned on 3D scene features. TCP4D uses TCP pose and gripper state as shared interface between motion tracking and action generation, tracking them across observed frames in 4D scene representation reconstructed from RGB video. Cross-Embodiment Augmentation Pipeline. Existing approaches to robot data augmentation include simulation-based demonstration synthesis (Mandlekar et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2024) and image-space semantic augmentation (Yu et al., 2023; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024b), which expand motion and scene diversity without additional real-world collection. For embodiment transfer, Mirage (Chen et al., 2024a) uses test-time cross-painting to present target robot as the source robot expected by pretrained policy. RoVi-Aug (Chen et al., 2024b) uses diffusion-based image generation to replace source-robot appearances with target embodiments while retaining the associated task-space motion. OXE-AugE (Ji et al., 2025) further scales embodiment augmentation through simulation-based trajectory retargeting, background inpainting, and target-robot rendering. However, RoVi-Aug and OXE-AugE assume access to recorded source end-effector poses and actions. In contrast, TCP4D recovers TCP trajectories in SE(3) and gripper states from RGB videos and obtains target joint configurations through IK, enabling augmentation without recorded source-robot states.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate TCP4D across four dimensions: (1) TCP tracking performance, (2) the effectiveness of cross-embodiment data augmentation, (3) robot manipulation performance of the TCP generator, and (4) real-world manipulation performance on physical robot platform. 4.1 Training Setup Datasets and Benchmark. We use the subset of DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) annotated by PointWorld (Huang et al., 2026a), comprising 33,966 episodes (67,932 camera sequences) of Franka Panda 7DOF Arm. We use 90% of the episodes for training and randomly sample 100 episodes from the remaining 10% as the evaluation set. For in-the-wild evaluation, we additionally collect 100 episodes spanning 100 distinct tasks in RoboLab (Yang et al., 2026b). To evaluate robot manipulation, we use RoboTwin (Chen et al., 2025) and collect 50 clean demonstrations per task for 48 tasks, using the thirdperson view. We train on these demonstrations and evaluate under both clean2clean and clean2random settings. Implementation Details. In Stage 1, we train two separate TCP trackers on DROID and RoboTwin, respectively, initializing their visual backbones and geometry modules from pretrained 4RC (Luo et al., 2026) weights. RGB image resolutions are 320 180 for DROID and 320 240 for RoboTwin. We sample Stage 1 clips with random starting frames, per-clip temporal stride randomly chosen from 15, and temporal reversal. In Stage 2, we use only RoboTwin data to train the TCP generator. Each sample contains = 4 consecutive observation frames paired with the next = 32 TCP states, preserving chronological order. The Stage 1 tracker and the full TCP4D model contain approximately 1.522B and 2.272B parameters, respectively, including frozen modules and retained heads. We report AbsRel, MAE, and δ1 for depth within 3 m; Average Percentage of Points (APD) and Mean Position Error (MPE) for 3D TCP tracking; Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE), Relative Rotation Error (RRE), and Relative Translation Error (RTE) for SE(3) tracking; and tracking Success Rate (SR). As shown in Table 1, TCP4D achieves state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated metrics across both benchmarks. On DROID and RoboLab, it achieves APD scores of 74.78% and 43.71%, respectively, more than four times those of the strongest baselines, and reduces ATE to 7.60 and 16.07 mm. TCP4D also achieves 100% SR on both datasets, successfully processing all evaluated tracking windows, compared with the best baseline SRs of 89.64% and 96.33%, respectively. Competing point-tracking methods rely on tracking rigid point groups and fitting rigid transformations in post-processing to recover TCP poses; inaccurate or inconsistent point tracks can yield unreliable pose estimates or prevent successful recovery. By directly predicting TCP poses and gripper states within unified feed-forward framework, TCP4D avoids this recovery step, delivering accurate and reliable tracking even in unseen manipulation scenarios. As shown in Fig. 6, combining source and augmented demonstrations improves Aloha performance on all four tasks, raising its mean success rate from 53.5% to 65.5%. Click Bell shows the largest improvement, from 30% to 52%, demonstrating the effectiveness of augmented demonstrations for policy learning on the source embodiment. On ARX-X5, joint training increases the mean success rate from 30.5% to 72.0% relative to augmented-only training. The gains span all four tasks, including Place Burger Fries (12% 78%) and Click Bell (14% 70%). On UR5-WSG, joint training improves the mean success rate from 32.0% to 39.0%, with gains on Place Burger Fries (28% 40%), Click Bell (42% 48%), and Handover Mic (8% 18%). These results show that our pipeline enables policy learning on target robots without original demonstrations from those embodiments, while also improving performance when augmented demonstrations are combined with existing data, highlighting the utility of TCP4D for cross-embodiment data augmentation. 4.4 TCP4D Manipulation Performance Results. We evaluate TCP4D on 48 RoboTwin tasks with 100 trials per task and report the success rates in Table 3. TCP4D achieves the highest reported average success rate of 69.19% under clean2clean. It surpasses established manipulation policies ACT, RDT, and DP3 by 39.94%, 35.27%, and 14.92%, respectively, and also outperforms several VLA models, including EventVLA (65.71%), GalaxeaVLA (62.73%), and π0 (45.21%). These results support the effectiveness of predicting future TCP motion from 4D scene representations and highlight the potential of this paradigm for robotic manipulation. Complete results for all 48 tasks are provided in Appx. F.1. The average success rate drops to 10.94% under clean2random, where environmental randomization introduces distribution shift. Our TCP generator is trained solely on clean demonstrations. Incorporating large embodiment data pretraining or 3D geometric data from broader mix of sources could improve 9 generalization to randomized environments, direction we leave for future work. As shown in Fig. 8, TCP4D outperforms DP3 and ACT on both real-world tasks in success rate and progress score. It achieves success rates of 83.33% on placing pens and 73.33% on stacking bowls. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented TCP4D, unified model using shared 4D scene representation to track TCP motion from RGB video and generate future actions conditioned on the recovered tracks. Our cross-embodiment pipeline converts videos into target-robot demonstrations. Experiments demonstrate accurate tracking, few-shot adaptation, effective manipulation, and improved policy learning with augmented data. TCP4D has the potential to scale up with more diverse data and robot embodiments.

Cross-Embodiment Augmentation B.1 Augmentation Pipeline TCP4D enables cross-embodiment augmentation by recovering task-space motion directly from RGB demonstrations. As illustrated in Fig. 3, the pipeline comprises motion recovery, embodiment retargeting, and visual composition. Given source video and initial TCP queries, TCP4D predicts TCP trajectories, gripper states, and camera geometry. The recovered poses are aligned in common coordinate frame 19 and transferred to the target robot through inverse kinematics using its kinematic model, producing joint configurations that follow the demonstrated task-space motion. We segment the source robot using SAM3 (Carion et al., 2026) or, when available, its geometric model and recorded states. ProPainter (Zhou et al., 2023) completes the masked regions to reconstruct the background. We then render the target robot at the recovered configurations and composite it into the completed frames using the aligned camera geometry. The resulting images are paired with target configurations to form augmented demonstrations. Depth from TCP4D can optionally improve segmentation quality or distinguish foreground and background, but the pipeline does not depend on depth. During Retarget, if IK fails at the target robots initial base placement, the pipeline automatically searches nearby robot-base translations and retries IK over the full trajectory (auto_base is enabled by default). The base orientation remains fixed during this search, and the target arm is accepted only when every frame passes IK. For further details on robot-base adjustment in cross-embodiment augmentation, refer to the OXE-AugE (Ji et al., 2025) paper and project page. Each minibatch contains fixed total of 18 frames per device. For each minibatch, we randomly choose the number of clips {1, 2, 3, 6, 9} and sample 18/S frames per clip, yielding the respective clip lengths 18, 9, 6, 3, and 2. Each clip comes from single camera stream, with temporal stride sampled uniformly from the feasible values in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and randomly chosen starting frame. The sampled stride is constant within clip and can differ across clips. Each clip is reversed with probability 0.5; images and all associated labels are reordered together. The first frame in the resulting sequence serves as the TCP query frame, so queries can originate at different points within an episode and support tracking in either temporal direction. Temporal supervision uses the signed time intervals between sampled frames, accounting for both subsampling and reversal. Clips remain within valid trajectory segments and do not cross detected discontinuities. Stage 2 Sampling. For each sample, we randomly choose current frame and use the four consecutive observations ending at as history (L = 4), with the following 32 TCP states as targets (h = 32). Sampling is strictly forward with unit temporal stride and no reversal. If fewer than four historical frames are available within the current valid segment, we repeat its earliest observed frame. If fewer than 32 future states remain, we repeat the last valid state for storage and mask the padded positions in attention and loss computation. The current robot state and wrist images are taken at t, and language instruction is sampled from those associated with the episode. C.3 Sliding Window Inference As illustrated in Fig. 10, TCP4D extends TCP tracking to long videos by propagating visual queries across overlapping windows. Only the initial frame requires 2D TCP queries for the available arms; subsequent windows use queries derived from the models recovered TCP positions. TCP Tracking. For example, the tracker processes 1 frame windows by default, with configurable length of 218 frames. Consecutive windows share exactly one boundary frame, so full 1 frame window advances the sequence by 2 frames; the final window can be shorter. After processing window, we project its final-frame 3D TCP positions into the shared boundary image using the camera intrinsics decoded from the ray map. These projected positions become the reference-frame queries for the next window, as shown in Fig. 10. 22 Figure 10: Sliding-window TCP tracking inference. TCP4D supports inference on sequences of varying lengths. To track long sequence, only the TCPs 2D location in the first frame needs to be specified. The predicted 3D TCP position, (x, y, z), at the final frame can then be projected onto the camera plane and used as the new query for the next window. Figure 11: Query points on DROID and Robolab for baseline evaluation. For baselines evaluated by rigid fitting of point tracks, we select 16 point groups on the gripper in the first frame of each window using ground-truth annotations, track them throughout the window, and fit the TCP pose from the tracked points. Conditional TCP Generation. For each window, we project the predicted TCP positions in the history frames into their corresponding images and sample local feature tokens from the shared visual representations. These tokens are fed into the DiT to condition future TCP generation.

sections.content: This section describes the datasets, protocol, and metrics used for the tracking evaluation in Table 1 and reports additional results. All TCP poses are expressed in the camera coordinate system of the corresponding frame. D.1 Datasets DROID. The PointWorld-annotated DROID subset contains 33,966 episodes. We use fixed episode-level split with seed 42, assigning approximately 90% of the episodes to training. From the remaining 10%, we randomly sample 100 episodes for evaluation. Each DROID episode has two third-person view cameras and is sampled at 15 Hz. RoboLab. The additional RoboLab set contains one episode for each of 100 distinct tasks and is used exclusively for in-the-wild evaluation. We use π0.5 (Intelligence et al., 2025) as the policy to generate trajectories, including both successful and failed trajectories. During data collection, we randomize the backgrounds and camera positions. RoboLab is sampled at 15 Hz. D.2 Evaluation Protocol Baseline Evaluation Windows. The 4RC (Luo et al., 2026), Any4D (Karhade et al., 2026), Track4World (Lu et al., 2026), VDPM (Sucar et al., 2026), MoSE3 (Cheng et al., 2026), and CoTracker3 (Karaev et al., 2025) baselines use independent, non-overlapping nine-frame windows, with potentially shorter final window. Each windows query frame is excluded from tracking metrics. TCP Pose Recovery from Point Tracks. For 4RC, Any4D, Track4World, VDPM, and CoTracker3, we recover TCP poses by rigid fitting of point tracks. As shown in Fig. 11, each window is initialized with ground-truth-projected points on the fixed Robotiq gripper body. Each query is associated with known surface point on the gripper URDF model, and this query-to-model correspondence is retained throughout the window. CoTracker3 uses VGGT-Ω depth predicted for every frame, together with the calibrated camera intrinsics, to lift its 2D tracks into 3D. For all these baselines, including CoTracker3, we calibrate the predicted 3D point groups scale using the known metric dimensions of the corresponding URDF points at window initialization and keep this scale fixed throughout the window. At each tracked frame, we robustly fit rigid transformation from the corresponding gripper model points to their scale-calibrated 3D predictions. The fitted rotation and translation describe the gripper bodys pose in that frames camera coordinates. We apply the known fixed body-to-TCP offset to recover the TCP position and use the fitted body rotation as the TCP orientation, consistent with the datasets TCP convention. Repeating this fit across frames converts the point-group tracks into TCP pose trajectory. MoSE3 Native SE(3) Motion Estimation. For MoSE3, we use its official rigidity-weighted per-point SE(3) estimation procedure. At the start of each window, we perform the same URDF-based scale calibration and rigid fitting to initialize the TCP pose from the predicted 3D point group. We then propagate this pose using the SE(3) motion associated with fixed gripper-surface query, selected as the query nearest the image-space mean of the group, and transform it into each frames camera coordinates using the predicted camera poses. The initialization scale is applied to both motion and camera translations. No additional CAD-to-track rigid fitting is performed at subsequent frames. sections.title: G Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Embodiment Coverage. While TCP4D demonstrates strong performance in DROID setting, its training data currently covers only embodiments with Franka and Robotiq grippers, and other embodiment data remains limited. After pretraining on DOIRD data, the TCP4D adapts effectively to UR5-WSG with only few demonstrations  (Table 2)  . These results support the use of shared SE(3) TCP representation for cross-embodiment transfer. With sufficient training data from diverse range of embodiments, we expect TCP4D to generalize well to new robot platforms and gripper designs. Environmental Generalization. The TCP4D Generator shows strong performance under RoboTwin clean2clean, but its performance under clean2random remains limited. The Generator is trained on relatively small set of clean demonstrations without large-scale policy pretraining, providing little exposure to the environmental variations encountered during randomized evaluation. This limited training diversity may partly explain the performance gap. Large-scale pretraining on diverse manipulation data, together with domain randomization and targeted data augmentation, offers practical directions for addressing this gap and realizing the broader potential of 4D-conditioned TCP generation.
